books.section: Topic 5.9 Government Policies During the Civil War
Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Frederick Douglass, “Men of Color, to Arms!” (March 1863)

stimulus.source_note: Frederick Douglass, “Men of Color, to Arms!”, speech delivered March 2, 1863, Rochester, New York, published March 21, 1863. Public domain. Wording verified against the BlackPast and National Park Service texts. “. . .” marks omitted text between passages, quoted in their order in the source.
stimulus.text:
“When first the rebel cannon shattered the walls of Sumter and drove away its starving garrison, I predicted that the war then and there inaugurated would not be fought out entirely by white men. . . . Liberty won by white men would lose half its luster. ‘Who would be free themselves must strike the blow.’ ‘Better even die free, than to live slaves.’”

—Frederick Douglass, “Men of Color, to Arms!”, speech in Rochester, New York, March 2, 1863

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Douglass’s call to arms and the enlistment of Black soldiers mattered to the Union war effort in two ways at once. Which pair best captures both?

options.text: It ended the draft in the North, and it freed enslaved people in the border states at once.
options.misconception: Background: the draft continued until the war’s end, and the border states kept slavery until the Thirteenth Amendment.

options.text: It added about 180,000 soldiers to Union ranks, and it tied the war’s purpose to freedom and citizenship.
It won British recognition of the Confederacy, and it ended the Union naval blockade.
options.misconception: Background: Britain never recognized the Confederacy, and the blockade ran until the war’s end.

options.text: It gave Black soldiers the vote at once, and it repealed the Fugitive Slave Act.
options.misconception: Background: Black men did not gain the vote nationwide until the Fifteenth Amendment in 1870, and the Fugitive Slave Act was repealed by Congress in 1864, not by enlistment.

rationales.A: Background: the draft continued until the war’s end, and the border states kept slavery until the Thirteenth Amendment.
rationales.C: Background: Britain never recognized the Confederacy, and the blockade ran until the war’s end.
rationales.D: Background: Black men did not gain the vote nationwide until the Fifteenth Amendment in 1870, and the Fugitive Slave Act was repealed by Congress in 1864, not by enlistment.
rationales.B: About 180,000 Black men joined Union ranks, and their service tied the war’s purpose to freedom and to a claim on citizenship.
rationales.general:
1. Count the soldiers first: about 180,000 Black men served in the Union army.
2. That is roughly one in ten Union soldiers, a real addition to Union strength.
3. Then weigh the meaning: Douglass ties service to citizenship, so the war becomes a war for freedom.
4. One enlistment does two jobs, military and moral, at the same time.
Remember: a policy that adds soldiers and changes the war’s meaning is doing double work.
